title: Second-highest salary
statement: Given an employees(id, name, dept, salary) table, return the name and salary of the second-highest paid employee in each department. If a dept has no second-highest (only one employee), exclude it.
hint: Window functions. DENSE_RANK vs RANK matters when there are ties.
solution:
with ranked as (
  select name, dept, salary,
    dense_rank() over (partition by dept order by salary desc) as rnk
  from employees
)
select name, dept, salary
from ranked
where rnk = 2;
explain: DENSE_RANK (not RANK) so two top earners in a dept still have a second-highest. Filter to rnk=2 to return the answer; departments without a rnk=2 row naturally drop out.

title: Dedupe by latest update
statement: From a CDC stream events(account_id, status, updated_at), return the most recent row per account_id.
hint: ROW_NUMBER + filter to 1. SELECT DISTINCT won't work — it dedupes by all columns.
solution:
with ranked as (
  select *,
    row_number() over (
      partition by account_id
      order by updated_at desc
    ) as rn
  from events
)
select * from ranked where rn = 1;
explain: The canonical CDC dedupe pattern. ROW_NUMBER picks exactly one row per key; ordering DESC by updated_at selects the most recent. Preserves all columns of the chosen row, unlike GROUP BY MAX.

title: Running total per customer
statement: From orders(customer_id, order_date, value), compute the running total of value per customer ordered by date.
hint: Frame the window: ROWS BETWEEN UNBOUNDED PRECEDING AND CURRENT ROW.
solution:
select customer_id, order_date, value,
  sum(value) over (
    partition by customer_id
    order by order_date
    rows between unbounded preceding and current row
  ) as running_total
from orders;
explain: The explicit ROWS BETWEEN frame is best practice. Without it, some engines default to RANGE which behaves unexpectedly on duplicate order_dates.

title: Top N per group
statement: From sales(rep_id, customer_id, revenue, sale_date), return the top 3 customers by total revenue for each rep.
hint: Two steps: aggregate per (rep, customer) first; then ROW_NUMBER over reps to take top 3.
solution:
with totals as (
  select rep_id, customer_id, sum(revenue) as total_rev
  from sales
  group by rep_id, customer_id
),
ranked as (
  select *,
    row_number() over (partition by rep_id order by total_rev desc) as rn
  from totals
)
select rep_id, customer_id, total_rev
from ranked
where rn <= 3;
explain: The classic top-N-per-group pattern. Aggregate first to define the ranking metric, then rank, then filter. Putting all three in one SELECT will silently fail or be unreadable.

title: Sessionization
statement: From events(user_id, event_ts), group events into sessions where consecutive events within 30 minutes belong to the same session. Output: user_id, session_id, started_at, ended_at, event_count.
hint: Two windows: (1) lag to compare current event to previous, (2) sum to assign cumulative session IDs.
solution:
with gaps as (
  select user_id, event_ts,
    lag(event_ts) over (partition by user_id order by event_ts) as prev_ts
  from events
),
sessions_marked as (
  select user_id, event_ts,
    sum(case when prev_ts is null
              or datediff('minute', prev_ts, event_ts) > 30
              then 1 else 0 end)
      over (partition by user_id order by event_ts
             rows between unbounded preceding and current row) as session_num
  from gaps
)
select user_id, session_num as session_id,
  min(event_ts) as started_at,
  max(event_ts) as ended_at,
  count(*) as event_count
from sessions_marked
group by user_id, session_num;
explain: Sessionization is a rite of passage. The key trick: a "new session" marker (1 or 0) summed cumulatively gives each session a unique increasing ID.

title: Detect fan-out
statement: You joined orders (1M rows) to order_items (5M rows) and now your SUM(orders.value) is 5× too large. Write a query that quantifies the fan-out factor per order.
hint: COUNT(*) GROUP BY order_id after the join. Compare to 1.
solution:
with joined as (
  select o.order_id, o.value, i.item_id
  from orders o
  left join order_items i on i.order_id = o.order_id
),
fanout as (
  select order_id, count(*) as rows_per_order
  from joined
  group by order_id
)
select
  count(*) as n_orders,
  sum(case when rows_per_order > 1 then 1 else 0 end) as n_with_fanout,
  avg(rows_per_order) as avg_fanout,
  max(rows_per_order) as max_fanout
from fanout;
explain: The diagnostic query you run BEFORE writing the aggregate. If avg_fanout > 1, your SUM is inflated; you must aggregate one side first.

title: Gaps and islands
statement: From availability(user_id, day) — one row per day a user was active — return consecutive date ranges per user: user_id, range_start, range_end, days.
hint: Classic gaps-and-islands. ROW_NUMBER + date subtraction creates a constant-per-island grouping key.
solution:
with with_grp as (
  select user_id, day,
    date_sub(day,
      row_number() over (partition by user_id order by day)) as grp
  from availability
)
select user_id,
  min(day) as range_start,
  max(day) as range_end,
  count(*) as days
from with_grp
group by user_id, grp
order by user_id, range_start;
explain: If days are consecutive, day - row_number() stays constant. Grouping by that constant gives you the islands. Stares at it long enough and it makes sense.

title: Pivot status counts
statement: From deals(account_id, status), return one row per account with three counts: open_count, won_count, lost_count.
hint: Conditional aggregation. SUM(CASE WHEN ... THEN 1 ELSE 0 END).
solution:
select account_id,
  sum(case when status = 'open' then 1 else 0 end) as open_count,
  sum(case when status = 'won'  then 1 else 0 end) as won_count,
  sum(case when status = 'lost' then 1 else 0 end) as lost_count
from deals
group by account_id;
explain: Portable pivot pattern that works in every SQL dialect. Beats PIVOT syntax for review-clarity.

title: Anti-join (find missing)
statement: Find accounts that have no rows in jobs table. Use the NULL-safe approach.
hint: NOT IN is NULL-trapped. Use NOT EXISTS or LEFT JOIN ... WHERE x IS NULL.
solution:
-- preferred: NOT EXISTS (NULL-safe)
select a.*
from accounts a
where not exists (
  select 1 from jobs j
  where j.account_id = a.account_id
);

-- equivalent: LEFT JOIN ... WHERE NULL
select a.*
from accounts a
left join jobs j on j.account_id = a.account_id
where j.account_id is null;
explain: Never use NOT IN (subquery) — if the subquery has any NULL, you get zero rows. Both alternatives are safe and correct.

title: Cohort retention table
statement: Given users(user_id, signup_date) and activity(user_id, active_date), build a cohort retention matrix: rows = signup month, columns = months since signup (0,1,2,...), values = % retained.
hint: Compute months_since_signup per active row. Aggregate per (cohort_month, months_since_signup) and divide by cohort size.
solution:
with cohorts as (
  select user_id, date_trunc('month', signup_date) as cohort_month
  from users
),
cohort_sizes as (
  select cohort_month, count(*) as cohort_size
  from cohorts group by cohort_month
),
activity_months as (
  select
    c.cohort_month,
    datediff('month', c.cohort_month, date_trunc('month', a.active_date)) as months_since,
    count(distinct c.user_id) as active_users
  from cohorts c
  join activity a on a.user_id = c.user_id
  group by c.cohort_month, months_since
)
select
  am.cohort_month,
  am.months_since,
  am.active_users,
  cs.cohort_size,
  am.active_users * 100.0 / cs.cohort_size as retention_pct
from activity_months am
join cohort_sizes cs on cs.cohort_month = am.cohort_month
order by am.cohort_month, am.months_since;
explain: Two-table reconciliation pattern. Cohort size is the denominator; active users at each month-since is the numerator. The "wide format" version comes from pivoting months_since in BI layer or another CASE-WHEN pivot.

title: Median per group
statement: Compute the median order value per customer without using MEDIAN() (some warehouses lack it).
hint: PERCENTILE_CONT or split via row_number + count.
solution:
-- Preferred: percentile_cont (Spark, Postgres, Snowflake)
select
  customer_id,
  percentile_cont(0.5) within group (order by value) as median_value
from orders
group by customer_id;

-- Without percentile_cont:
with ranked as (
  select customer_id, value,
    row_number() over (partition by customer_id order by value) as rn,
    count(*) over (partition by customer_id) as cnt
  from orders
)
select customer_id, avg(value) as median_value
from ranked
where rn in ((cnt + 1) / 2, (cnt + 2) / 2)
group by customer_id;
explain: Median = middle row(s). For even counts, average the two middle. The integer division (cnt+1)/2 and (cnt+2)/2 gives the right pair regardless of parity.

title: Funnel conversion
statement: From events(user_id, event_name, event_ts), compute the conversion funnel: visited → signed_up → activated → paid. Each step must happen AFTER the previous, per user.
hint: Self-joins via min(ts) per (user, step). Filter on ordering.
solution:
with first_step as (
  select user_id, event_name, min(event_ts) as first_ts
  from events
  where event_name in ('visited', 'signed_up', 'activated', 'paid')
  group by user_id, event_name
),
pivoted as (
  select
    user_id,
    max(case when event_name = 'visited'    then first_ts end) as ts_visited,
    max(case when event_name = 'signed_up'  then first_ts end) as ts_signed,
    max(case when event_name = 'activated'  then first_ts end) as ts_activated,
    max(case when event_name = 'paid'       then first_ts end) as ts_paid
  from first_step
  group by user_id
)
select
  count(*) as step_visited,
  sum(case when ts_signed    > ts_visited                          then 1 else 0 end) as step_signed,
  sum(case when ts_activated > ts_signed and ts_signed is not null then 1 else 0 end) as step_activated,
  sum(case when ts_paid      > ts_activated and ts_activated is not null then 1 else 0 end) as step_paid
from pivoted
where ts_visited is not null;
explain: Funnels need ordering: signed_up at 10am, then visited at 11am, doesn't count as conversion. Take min(ts) per (user, step), then conditionally count where each step is strictly later than the previous.

title: Incremental with merge
statement: Write an incremental model fct_events from stg_events. Use merge strategy with event_id as unique_key. Filter only new rows on subsequent runs based on updated_at with a 1-hour safety buffer.
hint: is_incremental() guards the filter. Subtract 1 hour from max watermark for late-arriving rows.
solution:
{{ config(
    materialized='incremental',
    unique_key='event_id',
    incremental_strategy='merge',
    on_schema_change='sync_all_columns'
) }}

with source as (
  select *
  from {{ ref('stg_events') }}
  {% if is_incremental() %}
    where updated_at > (
      select date_sub(max(updated_at), interval 1 hour)
      from {{ this }}
    )
  {% endif %}
)

select *, {{ audit_columns() }}
from source;
explain: merge + unique_key upserts cleanly. The 1-hour buffer catches late-arriving rows. on_schema_change auto-adds new columns instead of erroring.

title: Snapshot with check strategy
statement: Build a snapshot for dim_account_status that tracks changes to status and plan_tier over time. The source has no reliable updated_at.
hint: Use strategy: check with check_cols. dbt hashes the listed cols and writes a new version when they change.
solution:
{% snapshot account_status_snapshot %}
{{ config(
    target_schema='snapshots',
    unique_key='account_id',
    strategy='check',
    check_cols=['status', 'plan_tier']
) }}

select account_id, status, plan_tier, region
from {{ source('raw', 'accounts') }}
where __is_deleted = false
{% endsnapshot %}
explain: check strategy is for sources without timestamps — dbt computes a hash of check_cols per run and creates a new SCD2 version when it changes. dbt_valid_from / dbt_valid_to are added automatically.

title: Custom generic test
statement: Write a custom generic test positive_value that fails if any row has the tested column ≤ 0. Apply it to fct_orders.value.
hint: Generic tests live in tests/generic/ and take model + column_name. Failure = returning rows.
solution:
-- tests/generic/positive_value.sql
{% test positive_value(model, column_name) %}
select *
from {{ model }}
where {{ column_name }} <= 0
   or {{ column_name }} is null
{% endtest %}

# models/marts/_models.yml
columns:
  - name: value
    tests:
      - positive_value
explain: Generic tests are reusable assertions. Any column on any model can now use positive_value. Singular tests (one-off SQL files) are simpler but not reusable.

title: Macro to dedupe by latest
statement: Write a Jinja macro dedupe_latest(model, partition_by, order_by) that returns deduplicated rows keeping the latest per partition. Compose with ref().
hint: Just templates the standard ROW_NUMBER pattern. Macro returns SQL, doesn't run it.
solution:
-- macros/dedupe_latest.sql
{% macro dedupe_latest(model, partition_by, order_by) %}
  with _ranked as (
    select *,
      row_number() over (
        partition by {{ partition_by }}
        order by {{ order_by }} desc
      ) as _rn
    from {{ model }}
  )
  select * except (_rn)
  from _ranked
  where _rn = 1
{% endmacro %}

-- in any model:
{{ dedupe_latest(ref('stg_events'), 'event_id', 'updated_at') }}
explain: Macros DRY up repeated patterns. The dedupe-by-latest pattern shows up in every CDC pipeline — write it once, use it 50 times.

title: Slim CI selector
statement: In CI, your team wants to only build models that changed since main, plus everything downstream. Write the dbt build command.
hint: state: + + selector.
solution:
# With deferred state and selectors
dbt build -s state:modified+ --defer --state target/

# Breakdown:
#   state:modified  → models that changed since main
#   +               → also include downstream models
#   --defer         → use prod for unchanged refs (so you don't rebuild upstream)
#   --state         → location of the prod manifest.json for comparison
explain: Slim CI cuts PR build time 5–20×. The combination of state:modified+ + --defer is the magic — only build what you touched, but reference prod for everything else.

title: Source freshness
statement: Declare freshness checks on a SF Account source so dbt warns if it's not updated in 12 hours and errors after 24.
hint: config.freshness.warn_after + error_after + loaded_at_field.
solution:
# sources/src__salesforce/_salesforce__sources.yml
sources:
  - name: salesforce
    tables:
      - name: account
        config:
          loaded_at_field: _fivetran_synced
          freshness:
            warn_after: { count: 12, period: hour }
            error_after: { count: 24, period: hour }

# Run: dbt source freshness --select source:salesforce.account
explain: Freshness checks are how you catch upstream pipelines failing before they cascade. Add them at every source boundary.

title: Exposures + meta
statement: Declare an exposure for a Tableau dashboard "Sales Pipeline" that depends on fct_opportunities + dim_contractor_account. Owner: sales-analytics team.
hint: Exposures live in _exposures.yml. Type: dashboard.
solution:
# models/marts/_exposures.yml
version: 2
exposures:
  - name: sales_pipeline_dashboard
    type: dashboard
    label: "Sales Pipeline (Tableau)"
    url: "https://tableau.example.com/views/sales-pipeline"
    owner:
      name: Sales Analytics
      email: sales-analytics@example.com
    depends_on:
      - ref('fct_opportunities')
      - ref('dim_contractor_account')
    meta:
      audience: "sales-leadership"
      refresh_cadence: "hourly"
explain: Exposures make BI/external consumers visible in dbt's lineage graph. Critical for impact analysis ("if I change this model, what dashboards break?").

title: Project-level meta defaults
statement: Add a project-level configuration so every model in domains/contractor_account/marts/ inherits meta.owner: contractor-team and meta.layer: gold.
hint: dbt_project.yml supports +meta at directory level.
solution:
# dbt_project.yml
models:
  analytics:
    domains:
      contractor_account:
        marts:
          +meta:
            owner: contractor-team
            layer: gold
            contains_salesforce_data: true
          +materialized: table
          +tags: ['schedule__daily__morning']
explain: Cascading config saves you from setting the same values on every model. Note: this is MODEL-level meta only — column-level meta has no inheritance.

title: Test soft-delete asymmetry
statement: dim_account filters WHERE __is_deleted = false. fct_jobs keeps history of all jobs. Write a relationships test that catches orphan account_ids in fct_jobs WITHOUT failing on the known soft-delete asymmetry.
hint: relationships + where clause + severity warn.
solution:
columns:
  - name: account_id
    tests:
      - relationships:
          to: ref('dim_account')
          field: account_id
          config:
            severity: warn
            where: "event_date >= current_date - interval 90 days"
            error_if: ">1000"
            warn_if: ">0"
explain: Soft-delete asymmetry is unavoidable in some CDC patterns. The workaround: scope the test to recent data (last 90 days where the dim should still have the row), warn on any drift, escalate to error only if it explodes past a threshold.

title: API with retries
statement: Write a Python function fetch_page(url, params) that GETs the URL, retries up to 5 times on 429/5xx with exponential backoff, and raises on other errors.
hint: tenacity + requests. Define a retry predicate.
solution:
import requests
from tenacity import retry, wait_exponential, stop_after_attempt, retry_if_exception_type

class RetryableHTTPError(Exception): pass

@retry(
    wait=wait_exponential(multiplier=1, max=30),
    stop=stop_after_attempt(5),
    retry=retry_if_exception_type(RetryableHTTPError)
)
def fetch_page(url: str, params: dict) -> dict:
    r = requests.get(url, params=params, timeout=30)
    if r.status_code == 429 or r.status_code >= 500:
        raise RetryableHTTPError(f"HTTP {r.status_code}")
    r.raise_for_status()
    return r.json()
explain: Retry on transient (429, 5xx) but NOT on permanent errors (404, 401) — those will never recover and you'd waste 5 attempts. Exponential backoff prevents hammering recovering services.

title: Pandas → PySpark conversion
statement:
Convert this pandas snippet to PySpark: 
df = pd.read_csv('events.csv')
df = df[df['status']=='active']
top_users = df.groupby('user_id')['value'].sum().nlargest(10)
hint: Spark is lazy; transformations build a plan. F.col for column refs.
solution:
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

df = spark.read.csv("events.csv", header=True, inferSchema=True)
top_users = (
    df.filter(F.col("status") == "active")
      .groupBy("user_id")
      .agg(F.sum("value").alias("total"))
      .orderBy(F.col("total").desc())
      .limit(10)
)
top_users.show()   # action triggers execution
explain: Pandas executes eagerly; Spark builds a logical plan you execute with an action. filter → groupBy → agg → orderBy → limit all chain without running until .show().

title: Idempotent CLI script
statement: Write a Python CLI that takes --run-date and --full-refresh flags. Logs structured progress. Uses a date default of today.
hint: click for CLI, logging not print, date default via callable.
solution:
import click, logging
from datetime import date

logging.basicConfig(level=logging.INFO,
    format="%(asctime)s [%(levelname)s] %(message)s")
logger = logging.getLogger(__name__)

@click.command()
@click.option('--run-date', default=lambda: str(date.today()), help='YYYY-MM-DD')
@click.option('--full-refresh', is_flag=True, help='Rebuild from scratch')
def main(run_date, full_refresh):
    logger.info(f"Starting ETL for {run_date} (full_refresh={full_refresh})")
    rows = extract(run_date)
    logger.info(f"Extracted {len(rows)} rows")
    rows = transform(rows)
    load(rows, run_date, full_refresh=full_refresh)
    logger.info("Done.")

if __name__ == "__main__":
    main()
explain: lambda: str(date.today()) as default = "today" is computed at call time, not module import. Logger over print so output is timestamped and can be filtered by level.

title: Walk the dbt manifest
statement: Write a Python script that loads target/manifest.json and prints every FK-shaped column (ending in _id, _key) that doesn't have meta.join_to declared.
hint: manifest.json.nodes[].columns. Walk every model.
solution:
import json, re

fk_pattern = re.compile(r"_(id|key|uuid|sk)$")

with open("target/manifest.json") as f:
    manifest = json.load(f)

missing = []
for node_id, node in manifest["nodes"].items():
    if node.get("resource_type") != "model": continue
    for col_name, col_meta in node.get("columns", {}).items():
        if fk_pattern.search(col_name):
            if not col_meta.get("meta", {}).get("join_to"):
                missing.append((node["name"], col_name))

print(f"{len(missing)} FK columns missing meta.join_to:")
for model, col in sorted(missing)[:50]:
    print(f"  {model:50s} {col}")
explain: manifest.json is your project as data. Once you can read it, you can write CI checks, custom catalogs, and audit scripts.

title: Detect schema drift
statement: Given a Pandas DataFrame and an expected schema dict {col: dtype}, return a list of mismatches (missing cols, extra cols, type mismatches).
hint: Sets for missing/extra; dict-diff for type mismatches.
solution:
def schema_diff(df, expected):
    actual = {col: str(df[col].dtype) for col in df.columns}
    expected_cols = set(expected)
    actual_cols = set(actual)
    issues = []
    for c in expected_cols - actual_cols:
        issues.append(("missing", c, expected[c], None))
    for c in actual_cols - expected_cols:
        issues.append(("extra", c, None, actual[c]))
    for c in expected_cols & actual_cols:
        if expected[c] != actual[c]:
            issues.append(("type_mismatch", c, expected[c], actual[c]))
    return issues
explain: Three failure modes are distinct. Returning structured tuples (not strings) lets downstream code decide how to handle each — fail vs warn vs ignore.

title: Diagnose skew
statement: Your Spark job has 200 tasks. 199 finish in 30s; 1 takes 25 minutes. What's the diagnosis and what are your options?
hint: One outlier task = one partition with disproportionate data. Skew.
solution:
# Diagnosis: data skew. One key has ~50× more rows than others.
# Where it bites: groupBy or join key has a "heavy hitter" value.

# Option 1: Adaptive Query Execution (AQE) skew handling — auto split
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.enabled", "true")
spark.conf.set("spark.sql.adaptive.skewJoin.enabled", "true")

# Option 2: Salt the skewed key
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
skewed = skewed.withColumn("salt",
    (F.rand() * 10).cast("int"))
big = big.crossJoin(spark.range(10).withColumnRenamed("id", "salt"))
joined = skewed.join(big, ["key", "salt"])

# Option 3: If the other side is small, broadcast it
F.broadcast(small_table)
explain: Skew is the #1 cause of "Spark job hung." First check AQE (free). If still skewed, salt the heavy key into N buckets. Last resort: hand-optimise with broadcast hints.

title: Broadcast hint
statement: Your join is using SortMergeJoin when the dim table is only 8 MB. Force a broadcast hash join.
hint: F.broadcast(df) or SQL hint /*+ BROADCAST(t) */.
solution:
# PySpark
from pyspark.sql import functions as F
big_fact = spark.table("main.gold.fct_jobs")
small_dim = spark.table("main.gold.dim_account")

joined = big_fact.join(F.broadcast(small_dim), "account_id", "left")

# SQL equivalent
spark.sql("""
  SELECT /*+ BROADCAST(dim) */
    f.*, dim.region
  FROM main.gold.fct_jobs f
  LEFT JOIN main.gold.dim_account dim USING(account_id)
""")

# Verify with EXPLAIN — should show BroadcastHashJoin
explain: Spark's auto-broadcast threshold defaults to 10MB. If your dim is bigger but you know it fits in memory, hint it. The hint forces the planner; without it, missing stats cause a slow sort-merge.

title: Delta MERGE for upsert
statement: Write a PySpark snippet that upserts new jobs data into a Delta table main.gold.fct_jobs using job_id as the merge key.
hint: DeltaTable.forName(...).merge(...).
solution:
from delta.tables import DeltaTable
from pyspark.sql import functions as F

new_jobs = spark.read.format("delta").table("main.silver.stg_jobs")     .filter(F.col("__is_deleted") == False)

tgt = DeltaTable.forName(spark, "main.gold.fct_jobs")
tgt.alias("t").merge(
    new_jobs.alias("s"),
    "t.job_id = s.job_id"
) .whenMatchedUpdateAll() .whenNotMatchedInsertAll() .execute()
explain: MERGE is the idempotent operation. Run it twice with the same input, the result is identical. No INSERT bugs that double rows on retry.

title: Read query plan
statement: Given EXPLAIN FORMATTED output showing a SortMergeJoin + Exchange (shuffle) on a join you expected to broadcast, list 3 root-cause checks.
hint: Stats, size, hint syntax. Plan reading bottom-up.
solution:
Check 1: Are table stats current?
  ANALYZE TABLE main.gold.dim_account COMPUTE STATISTICS;
  Stale stats = Spark doesn't know the table is small.

Check 2: Is autoBroadcastJoinThreshold high enough?
  spark.conf.get("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold")
  Default = 10MB. If your dim is 11MB, no auto-broadcast.
  Bump it: spark.conf.set("spark.sql.autoBroadcastJoinThreshold", "100MB")

Check 3: Is the broadcast hint reaching the planner?
  EXPLAIN should show BroadcastExchange — if not, the hint was lost
  (often happens when you chain .join via a View or temp table).
  Move the broadcast as close to the join as possible.
explain: Reading Spark plans is a senior-AE skill. The 3 most common reasons "why no broadcast" are: stale stats, threshold too low, hint stripped by an intermediate node.

title: OPTIMIZE + ZORDER
statement: Your fct_events Delta table is 500GB, partitioned by event_date. Most queries filter by both event_date and user_id. Write the maintenance command + explain when to run it.
hint: OPTIMIZE compacts; ZORDER co-locates for high-cardinality cols.
solution:
-- co-locate user_id within each event_date partition
optimize main.gold.fct_events
where event_date >= current_date() - interval 7 days
zorder by (user_id);

-- Why partial optimize: re-clustering 500GB nightly is wasteful.
--   Recent partitions are queried most. Old partitions don't change.
--   Run nightly on last 7 days; full optimize quarterly.

-- Newer alternative: Liquid Clustering (Databricks 13.3+)
alter table main.gold.fct_events cluster by (user_id);
-- Databricks handles incremental re-clustering automatically
explain: OPTIMIZE = file compaction (small files → bigger). ZORDER = data sorting (faster filters). Run incrementally on hot data. Liquid Clustering removes the manual scheduling burden — newer projects should default to it.

title: Time travel for incident
statement: Yesterday at 3pm, someone ran a bad backfill on fct_revenue. Restore the table to its state at 2:50pm.
hint: Delta versions or timestamps.
solution:
-- See available versions
describe history main.gold.fct_revenue;

-- Read the pre-incident state
select * from main.gold.fct_revenue
timestamp as of '2026-05-19 14:50:00';

-- Restore — CAUTION: writes a new version
restore table main.gold.fct_revenue
to timestamp as of '2026-05-19 14:50:00';

-- VACUUM hasn't run? Then time travel still works.
-- VACUUM with 0 hours = unrecoverable. Don't.
explain: Delta's time travel is your audit + rollback. Files older than retention (default 7 days) are eligible for VACUUM — past that, can't recover. Always check DESCRIBE HISTORY before restoring.

title: Star schema for events
statement: Design a star schema for tracking job events in production. Source: a denormalized event log with columns (event_id, account_id, contractor_id, job_id, category_id, event_type, event_ts, value). What facts and dims would you build?
hint: Identify entities (dims) and events (facts). Be explicit about grain.
solution:
FACT TABLES (grain stated explicitly)

fct_job_events
  grain: one row per event_id
  cols: event_id (pk), event_type, event_ts,
        account_dim_key, contractor_dim_key, job_dim_key, category_dim_key,
        event_date_dim_key, value

fct_jobs_daily          # rollup for fast dashboards
  grain: one row per (job_id, date)
  cols: job_id, date, event_count, total_value, ...

DIMENSION TABLES

dim_account     (one row per account; SCD2 on plan_tier, status)
dim_contractor  (one row per contractor)
dim_job         (one row per job; SCD2 on status if status matters historically)
dim_category    (one row per category — small, slow-changing)
dim_date        (one row per calendar day; pre-built spine)

KEY DECISIONS
- Surrogate keys (dim_key) generated via md5 of (natural_key + valid_from)
- Foreign keys on facts point to surrogate dim keys (handles SCD2 versions)
- fct_job_events is event-level; fct_jobs_daily is the rollup
explain: The first decision in modeling is grain. Once that's locked, dims and facts fall out naturally. Pre-aggregating into a rollup fact (fct_jobs_daily) trades storage for query speed on common dashboards.

title: SCD Type 2 design
statement: dim_account holds contractor account info. Plan tier (Bronze/Silver/Gold) changes over time, and you need to attribute historical revenue to the tier the account was on at the time. Design the SCD2 columns and explain how facts join.
hint: valid_from / valid_to / is_current. Facts join on natural key + event date BETWEEN valid_from AND valid_to.
solution:
dim_account schema (Type 2 on plan_tier)
account_dim_key       -- surrogate, unique per (account_id, version)
account_id            -- natural key, NOT unique (multiple versions)
plan_tier             -- the value being tracked
status                -- also tracked
valid_from            -- when this version became active
valid_to              -- when superseded (NULL = current)
is_current            -- boolean shortcut, derived from valid_to

fct_revenue joining to dim_account at the historical tier:
select f.*, d.plan_tier
from fct_revenue f
left join dim_account d
  on d.account_id = f.account_id
  and f.event_date >= d.valid_from
  and (f.event_date < d.valid_to or d.valid_to is null)
explain: SCD2 = keep history with valid_from/valid_to. The fact joins by BETWEEN to grab the correct version-at-time-of-fact. Surrogate key avoids ambiguity when an account_id has multiple dim rows.

title: Avoid one-big-table
statement: A stakeholder asks for "one table with everything about an account." Make the case for and against the OBT pattern, then propose your decision.
hint: Convenience vs maintainability. Real warehouses have both, used differently.
solution:
PROS of OBT (one big table)
+ Stakeholders/BI tools love it — no JOINs needed
+ Performance can be great with columnar storage (only reads needed cols)
+ Self-documenting if columns are well-named

CONS of OBT
- Maintenance nightmare: every upstream change ripples to one place
- Permission/PII control is all-or-nothing on the table
- Grain ambiguity: "what's a row" depends on which join produced it
- Hard to evolve schema without breaking consumers

RECOMMENDED PATTERN
- Keep fact + dim as the canonical models (lineage clear, single grain)
- Build a "reporting" model alongside that JOINs them into a wide OBT
  for specific BI use cases (e.g., dashboard_account_overview)
- Mark the OBT clearly as a reporting layer artifact (not source of truth)

Example:
fct_revenue + dim_account + dim_contractor + dim_category
  ↓ (dashboard layer)
rpt_account_overview (OBT for stakeholder dashboard)
explain: OBT isn't evil — it's a reporting pattern. Use it as the LAST step, not the modeling philosophy. Keep facts + dims as the source of truth; wide tables for BI convenience.

title: Bridge table for many-to-many
statement: Contractors can be in multiple categories. Categories can have multiple contractors. Design the dimensional model so a fact (fct_leads) can attribute leads to one or many categories per contractor.
hint: Bridge table between dim_contractor and dim_category. Decide on weighting.
solution:
SCHEMA

dim_contractor     (one row per contractor)
dim_category       (one row per category)

bridge_contractor_category   -- many-to-many resolution
  contractor_dim_key
  category_dim_key
  weight              -- e.g., 1/N for equal split, or business-defined
  is_primary          -- one True per contractor if you want a "main" category

fct_leads
  lead_id
  contractor_dim_key   -- only contractor FK; category resolved via bridge
  ...

QUERY: leads attributed to each category (weighted)
select
  c.category_name,
  sum(f.value * b.weight) as attributed_revenue
from fct_leads f
join bridge_contractor_category b on b.contractor_dim_key = f.contractor_dim_key
join dim_category c on c.category_dim_key = b.category_dim_key
group by c.category_name;
explain: Many-to-many always needs a bridge. The weight column makes attribution explicit (split equally? proportional to lead volume? primary only?). Without weights, you risk multi-counting revenue.

title: Slowly changing... but mid-row
statement: A contractor account has 50 attributes. Only 3 of them are historically important (plan, manager, status). The other 47 should always be "current value." How do you design this?
hint: Type 6 hybrid. Or: split into Type 2 + Type 1 sub-dims.
solution:
OPTION A: Split into two dims
dim_contractor_current  (Type 1 — all 47 "live" attributes)
  account_id
  email, phone, billing_state, ..., 47 cols

dim_contractor_history  (Type 2 — only the 3 historical cols)
  account_dim_key (surrogate)
  account_id
  plan_tier, manager_id, status
  valid_from, valid_to, is_current

FACTS JOIN BOTH
fct_revenue
  ↓
  ─ joins dim_contractor_current via account_id  (gets latest email etc.)
  ─ joins dim_contractor_history via account_id + date BETWEEN ranges
                                              (gets historical plan/manager)

OPTION B: Type 6 (hybrid in one dim)
dim_contractor
  account_dim_key, account_id, ...           -- Type 2 cols
  current_email, current_phone, ...          -- Type 1: overwritten
  current_plan_tier, ...                     -- Type 3: prior value tracked

RECOMMENDATION
Option A is cleaner — separation of concerns, easier consumer SQL.
Option B is denser — fewer joins but harder to evolve.
explain: Real dims rarely fit neatly into a single SCD type. Splitting Type 1 (current) from Type 2 (historical) is a clean compromise that keeps each dim purpose-focused.

title: Real-time contractor dashboard
statement: Brief: "Show contractors their median lead-response-time vs peers, refreshed within 5 minutes." Sources: existing Kafka topics for lead-issued + contractor-response events. Design the end-to-end.
hint: Latency SLO is 5 min — that allows micro-batch, not full streaming. Use Spark Structured Streaming.
solution:
SOURCES
- Kafka topic: lead_issued (existing)
- Kafka topic: contractor_response (existing)

INGESTION
- Spark Structured Streaming reads both topics
- 5-minute trigger interval
- Exactly-once via Delta + idempotent Kafka offset tracking
- Write to bronze.lead_response_events (Delta)

SILVER (cleaned + joined)
- silver.lead_response_paired
  - Join lead + response by lead_id; stream-stream join with watermark
  - Add contractor + category dims (broadcast small dims)
  - Compute response_seconds = response_ts - lead_ts

GOLD (aggregated)
- gold.contractor_response_rolling30d
  - 30-day rolling median per (contractor_id, category_id)
  - dbt incremental every 5 min via Workflows

SERVING
- DBSQL Serverless warehouse
- AI/BI dashboard auto-refresh
- Or reverse-ETL to Postgres for in-product widget

DATA QUALITY
- unique on (contractor_id, lead_id, event_ts)
- not_null on contractor_id
- row count delta vs 1h ago must be within 30% (anomaly test)

TRADE-OFFS
- 5-min latency satisfies "real-time enough"
- Full streaming (Flink) would be ~3-5× more expensive for marginal latency gain
- Cost: ~$500/mo serverless DBSQL + ~$200/mo cluster for streaming job
explain: Match latency to actual SLO. "Real-time" almost never means sub-second; 5 minutes is usually fine and costs 1/3 as much as streaming. Structured Streaming is the sweet spot.

title: CDC pipeline architecture
statement: Design a CDC pipeline from MySQL prod (jobs, accounts) to Delta Lake. Handle inserts, updates, deletes correctly. Include schema evolution and DQ.
hint: Debezium → Kafka → Spark Streaming → Bronze → MERGE → Silver.
solution:
STACK
MySQL prod (jobs, accounts)
  ↓ binlog
Debezium connector
  ↓
Kafka (one topic per table, partitioned by PK)
  ↓
Schema Registry (Avro schemas, evolution rules)
  ↓
Spark Structured Streaming
  ↓ raw landing
Bronze Delta (append-only, all changes preserved)
  ↓ MERGE
Silver Delta (deduplicated, latest non-deleted row per PK)
  ↓
dbt models (Gold)

BRONZE WRITE
- One row per CDC event
- Cols: op (c/u/d/r), ts_ms, before, after, source.{db, table}
- Partitioned by event_date
- Used for replay + audit

SILVER MERGE LOGIC
WHEN MATCHED AND op='d' THEN UPDATE SET __is_deleted = true
WHEN MATCHED AND op IN ('c','u') THEN UPDATE all cols
WHEN NOT MATCHED AND op='c' THEN INSERT

SCHEMA EVOLUTION
- Schema Registry validates producer
- Delta MERGE WITH SCHEMA EVOLUTION auto-adds new cols in silver

DQ + MONITORING
- Source freshness: bronze updated < 5 min ago
- Row count: silver count = bronze (latest per PK, excl deleted)
- Schema drift: alert if new field appears in bronze that silver doesn't have
explain: CDC is the most common DE workload at modern companies. Bronze = full event log (replayable), Silver = current-state (what consumers want). The MERGE logic is where most bugs live — test it heavily.

title: Cost reduction
statement: Your Databricks bill is $80K/month. CFO wants 30% reduction without breaking SLAs. What's your investigation + reduction plan?
hint: Audit first, optimize second. Cluster sizing, scheduling, dead jobs, partitioning.
solution:
INVESTIGATION (week 1)
1. Query system tables: system.compute.warehouses_costs, system.access.audit
2. Top 20 most expensive queries — are they running daily, hourly, monthly?
3. Cluster utilization: avg CPU/memory across jobs (any over-sized?)
4. Auto-stop misconfig: any clusters running 24/7 unused?
5. dbt slim CI: are PR builds running --full-refresh?

QUICK WINS (week 2 — usually 15-20%)
- Enable auto-stop on all interactive clusters (10 min idle)
- Switch dev/test to serverless (pay-per-query, not per-hour)
- Reduce non-prod environments' uptime
- Drop unused dashboards/scheduled queries (audit before delete)
- Stop running dbt --full-refresh in CI; use state:modified+

MEDIUM (week 3-6 — another 10-15%)
- Right-size warehouses by p95 query latency (often 2x oversized)
- Add OPTIMIZE + Liquid Clustering to hot tables → query speedup
- Convert daily batch jobs running 24/7 to scheduled jobs

STRUCTURAL (week 6+)
- Move ML feature pipelines off prod cluster to dedicated cheaper one
- Negotiate enterprise discount with Databricks for committed spend

EXPECTED
30% reduction is achievable in 4-6 weeks with above; main resistance is
"don't touch X, it's important" — counter with: "we'll roll back if SLA breaches"
explain: Cost reduction is investigation-first. Audit usage data, find the 20% of compute driving 80% of spend, target those. Avoid blanket "shrink all clusters" — it breaks SLAs.

title: Multi-tenant data isolation
statement: Your warehouse holds data for 3 distinct stakeholder groups (Sales, Partnership, Contractors). Sales must not see Partnership's data. How do you enforce this in Unity Catalog?
hint: Catalog/schema level grants, dynamic views, row-level security.
solution:
LAYER 1: Catalog / Schema-level isolation
- main.sales.* — granted to sales-analysts group
- main.partnership.* — granted to partnership group
- main.shared.* — read-only common dims (dim_date, dim_geo)

GRANT USE CATALOG, USE SCHEMA, SELECT
  ON SCHEMA main.sales
  TO `sales-analysts`;

LAYER 2: Row-level security (dynamic views)
create view main.shared.contractor_view as
select * from main.shared.contractor_master
where case
  when is_account_group_member('sales-leads') then true
  when is_account_group_member('partnership') then partner_managed = true
  else false
end;

LAYER 3: Column masking for PII
alter table main.shared.contractor_master
alter column email set mask analytics.mask_email
  (using columns access_level);

LAYER 4: Audit + monitoring
- system.access.audit table: every query logged with user + tables touched
- Alert on group membership changes
- Monthly access review

ENFORCEMENT
- No raw SELECT from prod_data.* — only via curated catalogs
- meta.contains_pii flags fail builds if exposed to wrong catalog
explain: Unity Catalog's 3-layer model (catalog → schema → table) is the foundation. Layer dynamic views and column masking on top for fine-grained access. Audit is non-negotiable for SOC2/ISO27001.

title: Migration plan: DWH → Lakehouse
statement: Legacy DWH (Oracle, 8TB, 500 tables, 12 years old) needs to migrate to Databricks Lakehouse. Stakeholders rely on 60 dashboards. Plan a 6-month migration.
hint: Dual-run, prioritize by usage, contract-first migration.
solution:
MONTH 1: Foundations
- Set up Databricks workspace, Unity Catalog
- Establish CI/CD for dbt
- Land all 500 tables raw in bronze (Fivetran or scripts)
- No transformation yet — just shadow the source

MONTH 2: Prioritize
- Query log analysis: which 30% of tables drive 80% of consumer queries?
- Rank top 60 dashboards by usage; pick top 20 for migration sprint 1
- Map dashboards → upstream tables → required staging models

MONTH 3-4: Migrate Tier 1 (20 dashboards)
- Build dbt staging + intermediate + marts for these 20 dashboards' deps
- Dual-run: query both legacy DWH and new lakehouse from BI
- Reconcile row counts daily; investigate diffs
- Add data contracts on critical models

MONTH 5: Migrate Tier 2 (next 20 dashboards) + Switch BI to lakehouse
- Tier 1 stakeholders confirm lakehouse matches; cut over BI sources
- Build Tier 2

MONTH 6: Tier 3 + Decommission
- Final 20 dashboards
- Identify unused tables (no queries in 90 days) — don't migrate
- Read-only legacy DWH; sunset 60 days later

RISK MITIGATIONS
- Dual-run reduces "wrong number" surprises
- Tier-based migration ships value early
- Skip unused tables — saves 30-40% of work
- Stakeholder sign-off per tier prevents rollback
explain: Migrations are about prioritization and dual-running, not technology. Most legacy DWHs have 50% dead tables — migrating them is waste. Tier by usage, dual-run for reconciliation, sign off per tier.

title: Idempotency test
statement: Your daily DAG re-runs after partial failure. The output table has duplicates. Walk through the diagnosis + fix.
hint: Check INSERT vs MERGE. Check unique constraints. Check whether the re-run is truly re-running the same partition.
solution:
DIAGNOSIS
1. Is the load operation INSERT or MERGE?
   - INSERT: appends every run → duplicates expected
   - MERGE on unique_key: should overwrite → no dupes

2. Is the input data deterministic for the same run_date?
   - If source changed between runs (CDC stream), MERGE will resolve via latest

3. Is the DAG passing run_date as a parameter, or "today"?
   - "today" causes the re-run to land in wrong partition

FIX
- Switch INSERT to MERGE (Delta) or DELETE-then-INSERT for the partition
- Make sure ALL params are passed in, none derived from current time
- Add a unique constraint or test to catch dupes in CI

VERIFICATION
Run the job twice locally with the same --run-date.
Compare row counts before and after second run. Should be IDENTICAL.
explain: Idempotency = same input → same output, every retry. Bare INSERT breaks it; MERGE preserves it. The test: rerun and diff. If counts differ, you have a problem.
